Oilseeds, as sold from granulate I (experiment) had lead higher at 620 µg/kg, against 390 µg/kg for control (unamended soil, no granulate) in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/mozdzer2023-sludge-ash-granulates-crop-metals|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Ewa Mozdzer, Renata Gamrat · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/mozdzer2023-sludge-ash-granulates-crop-metals">The Effect of Sludge-Ash Granulates on the Content and Uptake of Heavy Metals by Winter Rape Seeds and Triticale</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Applied Sciences</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/mozdzer2023-sludge-ash-granulates-crop-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

on Food Additives 2022) to 501 µg/kg (Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives 2022).<sup class="cite">[[sources/jecfa-91st-cadmium-2022|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/jecfa-91st-cadmium-2022">Cadmium: rather than ordinary supply. Oilseeds, as sold from granulate IV (50% sludge, 20% ash), dose 3 (60 g/pot) (experiment) had nickel higher at 690 µg/kg, against 210 µg/kg for control (unamended soil, no granulate) in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/mozdzer2023-sludge-ash-granulates-crop-metals|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Ewa Mozdzer, Renata Gamrat · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/mozdzer2023-sludge-ash-granulates-crop-metals">The Effect of Sludge-Ash Granulates on the Content and Uptake of Heavy Metals by Winter Rape Seeds and Triticale</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Applied Sciences</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/mozdzer2023-sludge-ash-granulates-crop-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

For a buyer the practical points are the form bought, the basis a result is reported on, where the oilseeds came from and the laboratory’s reporting limit. Testing finds contamination but does not remove it.

<div class="hmi-analyte-explorer" id="hmi-occurrence-oilseeds" data-analyte-explorer data-compact-intro="true" data-source-summaries="true"><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-explorer-context><summary data-open-context aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-controls="hmi-occurrence-oilseeds-drawer">Comparison methods and scope</summary><div data-explorer-context-content>

<p>Each row is one statistic a source reports for one form of oilseeds, group and metal; percentiles, ranges and maxima reported for the same samples as a mean or median are shown on that row. Different forms and preparation states are kept apart, and dry-weight results never share a reference with as-sold or fresh-weight results. Ratings place a result against an HMI reference built from monitoring results and ordinary-setting medians for the same form and basis. Same-study contrasts compare a contaminated or treated site with its control, targeted with random sampling, a prepared form with the unprocessed one, or one group of a study with the median of its other groups. Held rows failed a check against their own source and are shown but not compared.</p>

<a id="sources-and-contamination-pathways"></a>
## How metals reach oilseeds

<a id="hmi-ing-010"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-root-uptake-surface-deposition-feed-transfer-or-other-biological-pathways"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-011"></a>
<a id="what-contamination-can-arise-from-agricultural-inputs-harvesting-processing-equipment-or-packaging"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-012"></a>
<a id="which-source-attribution-claims-are-measured-modelled-inferred-or-unresolved"></a>

The evidence on how metals reach oilseeds comes from studies that compared exposed and ordinary settings. Oilseeds, as sold from granulate IV (50% sludge, 20% ash), dose 3 (60 g/pot) (experiment) had nickel higher at 690 µg/kg, against 210 µg/kg for control (unamended soil, no granulate) in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/mozdzer2023-sludge-ash-granulates-crop-metals|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Ewa Mozdzer, Renata Gamrat · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/mozdzer2023-sludge-ash-granulates-crop-metals">The Effect of Sludge-Ash Granulates on the Content and Uptake of Heavy Metals by Winter Rape Seeds and Triticale</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Applied Sciences</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/mozdzer2023-sludge-ash-granulates-crop-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

These are observational comparisons from single studies; the size of the difference depends on the site, metal and distance.

<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How do heavy metals get into oilseeds?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

In the studies available, oilseeds from contaminated or exposed settings carried more metal than oilseeds from the same study’s control.<sup class="cite">[[sources/mozdzer2023-sludge-ash-granulates-crop-metals|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Ewa Mozdzer, Renata Gamrat · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/mozdzer2023-sludge-ash-granulates-crop-metals">The Effect of Sludge-Ash Granulates on the Content and Uptake of Heavy Metals by Winter Rape Seeds and Triticale</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Applied Sciences</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/mozdzer2023-sludge-ash-granulates-crop-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Oilseeds, as sold from granulate I (experiment) had lead higher at 620 µg/kg, against 390 µg/kg for control (unamended soil, no granulate) in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/mozdzer2023-sludge-ash-granulates-crop-metals|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Ewa Mozdzer, Renata Gamrat · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/mozdzer2023-sludge-ash-granulates-crop-metals">The Effect of Sludge-Ash Granulates on the Content and Uptake of Heavy Metals by Winter Rape Seeds and Triticale</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Applied Sciences</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/mozdzer2023-sludge-ash-granulates-crop-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="which-regions-report-the-lowest-levels-in-oilseeds" data-anchor="which-regions-report-the-lowest-levels-in-oilseeds" data-question="Which regions report the lowest levels in oilseeds?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Which regions report the lowest levels in oilseeds?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Among GEMS/Food reporting regions, oilseeds, as sold had the lowest lead subgroup median in PAHO (10 µg/kg) and the highest in WPRO (98 µg/kg); reporting regions are markets, not growing areas.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> For cadmium, the lowest regional median was in EURO (6 µg/kg) and the highest in EURO (1,100 µg/kg).<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-much-of-the-arsenic-in-oilseeds-is-inorganic" data-anchor="how-much-of-the-arsenic-in-oilseeds-is-inorganic" data-question="How much of the arsenic in oilseeds is inorganic?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How much of the arsenic in oilseeds is inorganic?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Inorganic arsenic, the more toxic form, was measured in 7 results from 2 sources, far fewer than total arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs|8]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) · 2014</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Dietary exposure to inorganic arsenic in the European population</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal 2014;12(3):3597</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) 2014 reported inorganic arsenic at 24.3 µg/kg (mean) in oilseeds, as sold from European dietary-survey occurrence data.<sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs|8]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) · 2014</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Dietary exposure to inorganic arsenic in the European population</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal 2014;12(3):3597</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>
